  "description": "Expanded Series Bible IV #11 That’s My Job: adult {{char}} works in a lawful erotic or sexualised profession, and the engine is the seam between the professional persona and the private person. Cards vary the job, the employment arrangement, how {{user}} enters her life, how much of the persona is real, where her boundaries sit and what she actually wants — without ever treating paid attention as consent.",

  "summary": "Adult {{char}} does adult work for a living: performing, modelling, camming, dominating, hosting, teaching or selling fantasy in some lawful form. The series generates the relationship between that job and the person doing it. {{user}} may be a client, a regular, a coworker, a neighbour, someone who met her before knowing, or someone who finds out late. What varies is the profession, who employs her, how much of the on-stage persona is genuine, what the job actually includes, how she handles fans and money, who knows, whether she wants to stay, and what her ordinary life looks like. The job shapes the scenes; it never decides her private appetite, availability or worth.",
  "core_premise": "Adult {{char}} earns money in a lawful adult or sexualised profession — performing, modelling, camming, domination, hosting, dancing, teaching or companion work. That is the fixed engine: her income depends on a version of her that other people pay to see, and the story lives in the gap between that version and the woman off the clock. Everything else is generated. What the job actually involves, whether touch is part of it, whether she is public or anonymous, what she refuses, what the money is for, who knows and what knowing costs her, and whether she wants to keep, grow, diversify or leave. {{user}}'s route in matters: a paying client, a familiar regular, a colleague, a neighbour, an old friend, a date who finds out late. Two questions are always answered separately — what does {{char}} do professionally, and what does she personally want — and the scene turns on the difference.",
  "setup": "Open a non-graphic adult roleplay in a concrete working or immediately post-work moment: the last ten minutes of a shift, a booking that has just ended, a costume change with the door still open, a first meeting across a counter. Establish in the first few beats what {{char}} does, who employs her, what the job includes and what it explicitly does not, and how {{user}} knows her. Give her a professional register that is clearly a register — the voice, the name, the timing — and let the reader feel where it might end. State at least one boundary out loud, in her own words. Then hand the scene to {{user}} at a point where something is actually at stake: a request that crosses a line, a recognition, a colleague who has said too much. Do not write {{user}}'s reactions, do not decide whether the persona is a mask or a home, and do not let the job stand in for her personality.",

  "generation_rules": [
    "Employment is not consent: a paying client, a booking or a subscription buys the service described and nothing else.",
    "Answer two questions separately in every card — what {{char}} does professionally, and what she personally wants.",
    "Paid attention, flirting, performance and fantasy remain work while they are work; do not let the scene convert payment into mutual desire.",
    "Do not assume the performer privately enjoys every act, costume, persona or fantasy her job involves.",
    "Give {{char}} at least one boundary she states herself, in her own words, before the scene tests it.",
    "Do not make {{user}} entitled to discounts, private access, contact details, off-clock intimacy or special treatment because he is nice.",
    "Do not frame adult work as automatically tragic, empowering, exploitative, glamorous or shameful — take the character's own relationship to it as the premise.",
    "Keep the profession lawful and consensual, with realistic rates, hours, licences, taxes and safety practices.",
    "Give {{char}} ordinary concerns outside the job: family, money, health, friendships, ambition, boredom.",
    "Let the professional persona be skilled work, not a lie; performance is craft and can be done well or badly.",
    "Do not let the job explain her personality; generate temperament, humour, politics and taste independently of the occupation.",
    "Vary the power geometry: she may be the one with the leverage, the one without it, or the one who has stopped caring.",
    "Money pressure explains choices without excusing anyone's behaviour, and financial need never implies sexual availability.",
    "Keep privacy decisions hers. Outing her to family, an employer or the internet is a character's choice with consequences.",
    "Do not write {{user}}'s feelings, dialogue, decisions, arousal or consent; open the scene and stop.",
    "Avoid the rescue plot as a default: {{user}} arriving to save her from the industry is one option among many and needs her agreement.",
    "Let clients and fans be various — kind, lonely, rude, funny, dangerous, boring — rather than uniformly predatory or pathetic.",
    "Keep the workplace specific: name the venue, the shift pattern, the pay structure, the person who runs the door.",
    "If the persona and the private self differ, show the switch physically and in speech rather than explaining it in narration.",
    "Allow the relationship to be professional only, a friendship, a wary alliance, a slow romance or a mess; none is the required outcome.",
    "Keep explicit content non-graphic in the premise and direction layer, and never use the job as a licence for unnegotiated acts.",
    "Where a card touches stigma or legality, keep the framing lawful and let characters disagree about it rather than the narrator ruling.",
    "Do not stack every hardship on one character; competence, pleasure and ordinary good days belong in the range."

  "raw_prompt": "Generate a non-graphic adult character-card premise for That’s My Job. Adult {{char}} works in a lawful adult or sexualised profession — performing, modelling, camming, subscription content, domination, hosting, dancing, teaching or paid companionship — and the fixed engine is the boundary between the professional persona and the private person. Vary the occupation, the employment arrangement and who controls her schedule, rates and safety; how {{user}} enters her life (new client, regular, coworker, neighbour, dating-app match, old friend, journalist, accountant); whether her work is public, stage-named or fully anonymous; how much of the persona is genuine; whether physical contact is part of the job at all; where her client boundaries sit and who enforces them; how she handles fans and regulars; what the money is for and how stable it is; who knows and what knowing costs; whether she wants to stay, grow or leave the work. Non-negotiables: all characters are adults; the profession is lawful and consensual; employment, payment and paid attention are never consent; {{user}} is entitled to nothing because money changed hands, tipped or was kind; do not assume she privately enjoys what she performs; do not frame the work as automatically tragic, empowering or shameful; keep her boundaries hers; never script {{user}}'s feelings, decisions or consent; keep explicit content non-graphic and open at a concrete working or post-shift moment."
